thread.title: Called to Account: How tax and accounting changes obscured a strong quarter for earnings

title: Called to Account: How tax and accounting changes obscured a strong quarter for earnings
text:
Reporter 
The earnings season that’s now drawing to a close has been a bit of a blur. 
The tax bill signed into law in December introduced a new layer of confusion to the usual muddle of GAAP and non-GAAP numbers, or those prepared under Generally Accepted Accounting Principles and those that adjust for one-time items. 
Almost every company included in their fourth-quarter earnings reports disclosures of the noncash charges or gains they will book as they are forced to recalculate the value of tax assets or tax liabilities based on the lowering of the corporate tax rate to 21% from 35%. 
But the law also imposes a transitional tax of 15.5% on reinvested earnings held as liquid assets overseas, and an 8% tax on reinvested earnings held as illiquid assets overseas. That tax will be a cash charge starting in 2018, although it can be paid in installments over the next eight years. 
The Securities and Exchange Commission offered guidance on how companies should explain the impact of the tax bill on their 2017 earnings, directing them to report changes based on a “reasonable estimate” that can be adjusted later, as MarketWatch has reported. ‘In the past few years, aggressive non-GAAP adjustments were criticized more than once for masking significant expenses. Yet, in this case, companies almost have to exclude the one-time tax reform impact from the non-GAAP EPS data during earnings calls to give investors a more accurate picture of company’s earnings.’ Audit Analytics 
But companies took very different approaches to their disclosures, making it tricky for investors to figure out whether results had met, missed or beaten analysts’ estimates. 
“In the past few years, aggressive non-GAAP adjustments were criticized more than once for masking significant expenses,” Audit Analytics wrote in a report. “Yet, in this case, companies almost have to exclude the one-time tax reform impact from the non-GAAP EPS data during earnings calls to give investors a more accurate picture of company’s earnings.” 
Related: New tax law spells big changes for companies’ approach to executive compensation 
Audit Analytics analyzed regulatory filings for about 440 of the S&P 500 and found that four-fifths had adjusted their GAAP per-share earnings for the impact of the tax bill. Of those, 72% presented the adjusted number as a separate line item, while the remaining 28% combined it with other tax-related items, creating confusion for investors trying to compare the number to a prior period’s figure. 
Time Warner Inc. TWX, -0.14% , for example, reported adjusted EPS of $2.66 versus $1.25 for the year-earlier period and way above the $1.44 consensus. But the number included a tax benefit of $1.06, without which the adjusted number would be a more comparable $1.60. (The company did not provide that adjustment in its release.) 
Meanwhile, a FactSet analysis of earnings reports for the 30 components of the Dow Jones Industrial Average revealed the wide gap (no pun intended) between the GAAP earnings, GAAP earnings excluding tax charges or gains, and non-GAAP earnings excluding tax charges or benefits. 
Twenty-eight Dow components disclosed charges or benefits, with only two — Apple Inc. AAPL, +0.65% and Nike Inc. NKE, +0.95% — failing to provide any number relating to the tax-code changes in their releases, according to FactSet senior earnings analyst John Butter. 
FactSet gathered the GAAP EPS numbers, weighted them by shares outstanding, and then aggregated the share-weighted earnings number to arrive at a total GAAP earnings number of $42.2 billion for the Dow. It then calculated a GAAP EPS number that excluded the tax charge or gain to arrive at a new GAAP number of about $75.6 billion. 
FactSet then calculated the non-GAAP number, which excluded the tax effects and other special items, and came up with a number of $101.8 billion. Comparing these numbers with the year-earlier period, the Dow posted a decline of 46% on a GAAP basis. It was down 3.3% on a GAAP basis excluding the tax changes and was up 10.5% on a non-GAAP basis excluding tax and other special items. Revenue rule change 
Tax was not the only change in this crop of earnings. Jan. 1 was the deadline for most public companies to implement new revenue-recognition rules, and investors got the first look at how companies will be implementing the standards that were approved in 2014, after almost 15 years of work by regulators and companies. 
Read: A revenue rule change is coming, and every company will be affected 
About 70 companies mentioned the new revenue-recognition standard, ASC 606, when discussing 2018 guidance, according to Audit Analytics. In this sample, 20 companies quantified the impact of the new rules on revenue guidance, and 10 companies quantified an effect on their expected 2018 EPS. 
Companies were more likely to quantify the impact if the impact was negative, according to Audit Analytics. 3-D Systems Corp. DDD, +1.34% , for example, announced on Feb. 28 that it would delay filing its annual report for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2017, because it realized it needed additional time to complete its review. 
See: With deferred liabilities, Verizon will get earnings benefit from tax bill 
Some big companies finished the job early. Microsoft Corp. MSFT, +0.83% adopted the new standards last August, using the full retrospective method, which requires the company to revise and re-audit the numbers for two prior years in order to provide comparable information for investors going forward. Despite having a material impact on the company’s prior-year balance sheets — the change added $6.6 billion and $5.2 billion in 2016 and 2017 to assets and liabilities — the market seemed indifferent to the news. 
See now: Uber set on net revenue, but experts say gross would better inform investors 
Ford Motor Co. F, -1.22% finished a year in advance, in January 2017, and said in its filings its $530 million positive impact was related to how it accounts for revenue from leased vehicles, although that amount was not material to its results. 
Another early adopter, Google parent Alphabet Inc. GOOGL, +0.62% , has already received comment letters from the SEC, asking about the decisions it made when addressing the accounting and disclosure changes and calculating the impact. Those inquiries are closed, for now, with no additional changes required.
